newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin urges safe sex as Russia faces AIDS crisis.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin urges safe sex as Russia faces AIDS crisis.

text.p: Have sex, but use a condom -- was the message to young Muscovites from the Kremlin on Thursday as Russia's health ministry and an international charity teamed up to launch a high-profile AIDS awareness campaign.

Once protected from the world's new killer disease by impermeable Soviet frontier controls, Russia is now on the verge of a major epidemic. The rate of infection with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has rocketed in the past year, officials said.

The "Safe Sex, My Choice" advertising campaign, targeting 15-24 year-olds in the capital, is a far cry from the days when the boast "There is no sex in the Soviet Union!" passed into popular culture as an ironic nod to the supposed victory of communist prudery over the Western sexual revolution of the 1960s.

But the alarming casualty figures have shocked the authorities into accepting the help of the charity Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors without Borders) to adapt successful techniques from abroad in order to prevent a major disaster.

"The outlook is extremely pessimistic," Alexander Goliusov, chief specialist at the Health Ministry's AIDS prevention department, told a news conference. "HIV infection is a problem of national security for Russia."
Up to 800,000 of Russia's 150 million people could be infected by the year 2000 compared with just a few thousand now, according to a health expert quoted by Medecins sans Frontieres.

In the first five months of 1997 alone, the number of people officially recorded as infected with HIV increased by nearly 80 percent. Last year, new cases exceeded the total for the previous nine years, since the first case was diagnosed in the Soviet Union.
The number of recorded cases is still small -- 4,494 people at the end of May, 259 of them with AIDS itself. But Goliusov said the real figure was probably two or three times that.
And he warned that the days when Russians could regard AIDS as a foreigners' plague were coming to an end.
"The current situation is very sharply different," Goliusov said. "Russia has entered a new phase of the epidemic."

Although at present 76 percent of HIV sufferers in Russia are intravenous drug users, the potential for rapid growth through sexual contact is underlined by an astonishing 60-fold increase in syphilis infection over the past eight years.
In 1988, syphilis was about as rare in the Soviet Union as in western Europe. Now, nearly 400,000 Russians are infected.

Officials hope the Moscow anti-AIDS campaign, which follows earlier national programmes, will be a pilot for other regions. In the worst hit city, Kaliningrad, the growth of HIV infection this year is projected to be nearly twice as high as in Los Angeles. The Baltic port is a crossroads for the drug trade.
Medecins sans Frontieres is promoting separate targetted programmes to educate young drug users -- estimated at 100,000 in Moscow alone -- and training schemes for medical workers.

The "Safe Sex, My Choice" slogan will be promoted by a television spot featuring typical teenagers and accompanied by pulsating music. It will also be carried on buses, billboards and in the press in an effort to convince young people, already well aware of the disease, to use condoms to protect themselves.
In a country where most adults smoke and hardly anyone wears a seatbelt, getting people to care for their health is not easy.
"People are fairly well informed of the dangers of AIDS, Goliusov said. "But, as with smoking and alcohol, the difficulty is bridging the gap from knowledge to actually doing something."

If the campaign succeeds, the biggest winners may be foreign condom makers. The health ministry wants to help Russian plants convert production lines from heavy-duty Soviet-era sheaths, nicknamed "galoshes", to produce gossamer-thin western condoms.
"The thing is the government hasn't got the money. So foreign manufacturers dominate the market," Goliusov said.
